hypothesis: Batch amortisation cannot be the source of an index-calculus advantage over rho, because rho amortises across a batch at least as well. Concretely: the Riemann-Roch solver's target-independent setup is real and does amortise across k targets, but its per-target cost has a strictly positive floor, while multi-target rho's per-target cost falls as 1/sqrt(k) without bound. Therefore a batch of size k cannot create a crossover that does not already exist at k = 1, and a batch win measured against k INDEPENDENT rho runs is an artefact of the wrong baseline.
motivation: A parallel session reported that sharing index-calculus setup across 16 targets used about 28% fewer instructions and 22% less time than running the existing rho solver separately for each target, while a single target cost 7.8% more instructions than rho. 'Separately for each target' is the baseline under test here. This experiment supplies the control that comparison is missing and states what would have to be true for a batch result to mean anything.
baseline: Multi-target / amortised rho, by the same law the repository already enforces elsewhere (src/ecc_safety.rs check_multi_target_margin, Galbraith-Lin-Scott / Kuhn-Struik): k discrete logarithms in one group of order r with one shared generator cost about sqrt(k*r) in total, so per-target cost is the single-target reference divided by sqrt(k). The single-target reference is the repository's own rho line for ECC2K-130 with the <-1> x <pi> speed-up: 2^60.8090 group operations, S = 0.077430.
measurement: At n = 131 and d in {6, 7} on the ECC2K-130 curve, split the quadratic-image solver's counted field API operations into (a) target-INDEPENDENT setup: the images of T_u(w) = w^2 + u*w on V for every nonzero u in V, which depend only on V; (b) target-DEPENDENT setup: the per-target geometry and batch inversions, which depend on x(R); (c) search and support/extract/verify. Batched per-target cost is then (a)/k + (b) + (c). Report the k -> infinity floor, which is (b) + (c).
independence_check: The image-space construction is re-implemented independently in this folder and asserted to reproduce solver_08's frozen Search.images exactly, for every nonzero u in V, at every panel dimension. solver_08 is not modified. If the two disagree the run is a correctness failure and no cost split is reported.
coverage: Also instantiate the coverage bound that governs the other direction of the same tradeoff: with a stored factor base of B points and three summands, at most C(B+2,3) distinct points are representable, so a uniformly sampled target of the order-r subgroup decomposes with probability at most min(1, C(B+2,3)/r). Report that bound at the measured base sizes and the B at which it reaches 1.
structural_limits: Two limits of the RR family are read off its own construction rather than measured, and are reported as structural: (1) ARITY IS FIXED AT THREE. The encoding lives in L(4O) with f = x^2 + a*x + c + b*y; div(f) = (P1)+(P2)+(P3)+(-R)-4(O) exhausts pole order four, so 'more summands' is not a parameter of this solver -- it needs a different Riemann-Roch space, not a different setting. (2) THE FACTOR BASE MUST BE AN F2-SUBSPACE. Both support tests are subspace tests: solver_05 divides by the subspace polynomial L_V, solver_08 tests membership in the image of the F2-linear map w -> w^2 + u*w on V. A normal-basis Hamming-weight factor base is not an F2-subspace, so it is outside this encoding entirely, not merely untested by it.
falsification: The batch claim of this contract is falsified if the measured target-independent share is large enough that the per-target floor (b)+(c) sits below the amortised rho line at any k -- i.e. if there is a k where batched RR beats batched rho but k = 1 does not. It is also falsified if the independent image-space re-implementation disagrees with solver_08.
limits: This prices an ORACLE, not an attack: at d in {6, 7} the factor base is far below the existence threshold (d = 45 at m = 3), so no relation yield, no linear algebra and no full-DLP S is measured or claimed here. The rho comparison is therefore a comparison of a per-target ORACLE floor against a per-target FULL SOLVE, which is generous to the RR side by construction -- the real attack additionally pays for relation collection and linear algebra. Counted field API operations in the Python ONB model are not calibrated against the repository's Rust/GPU cost model or against 'instructions', so the numeric ratios to rho are order-of-magnitude statements about the SHAPE of the two curves in k, not a like-for-like operation count. The sqrt(k) rho law is the standard amortisation result under its usual assumptions (one group, one shared generator, k targets); it is not re-measured here.
